(CNN)  -- First trip to Malmo? Here's some insider advice to help you get the most out of your visit. Locals like to take a cold dip after a sauna at Ribersborgs Kallbadhus. Getting around town Most of Malmo's attractions are reachable by foot, but flat terrain and an abundance of cycle paths also make the city ideal to explore by bike. Rentals run around 120 kronor. You can also jump on the eco-friendly buses that criss-cross the city. Visit the tourist office at Central Station for maps. If you opt for a taxi, be sure to set the price of the trip with the driver before setting off. Ice cool  For more than a century, locals have been visiting the Ribersborgs Kallbadhus for a steam in the sauna followed by a dip in the Baltic. The swimming baths are open year-round. If you want to blend in with the locals, brave the elements and hit the baths in the winter for an icy plunge. A better time to visit for the less adventurous is in the summer, when the baths are open for sunbathing. Living green  As part of its post-industrial transformation, Malmo has become a leader in environmental design. The city's green achievements are reflected by the Bo01 housing development, a waterfront regeneration project with a focus on environmentally-friendly living. For the latest in green design, visit the Western Harbor and Augustenborg neighborhoods. For a more informed look, contact the local Environmental Department, which occasionally offers free guided tours of the city's ecologically sustainable areas. Around the Sound  Malmo is located just 35 minutes by train from the Danish capital of Copenhagen, and every day thousands travel between the two cities via the Oresund Bridge. Trains leave from Malmo every 20 minutes for most of the day. After midnight, service is less frequent. The two cities are part of Scandinavia's Oresund region -- the transnational area made up of southern Sweden and eastern Denmark. The best way to explore the Oresund region is with an "Around the Sound" ticket, which gives you access to all the trains you need to travel around the area, including the ride across the Oresund Bridge. You can make as many stops as you want as long as you travel in one direction. Tickets are good for two days and also get you discounts to the major attractions in the region. Prices depend on how far you travel and start from 199 kronor. Feasting on crayfish  Swedes are crazy about crayfish, and outdoor festivities celebrating the crustacean are held across the nation to mark the end of summer. In Malmo, head to Stortorget, the city's main square, for one of the biggest crayfish parties in the world. The massive celebration is held annually to kick off the popular Malmo Festival. Swedes like their crayfish cooked in salty water infused with dill. Blend in with the locals by eating it cold with toast and beer. To really get into the tradition, wash down the crayfish with akvavit, a Scandinavian kind of vodka.

(CNN) — Visiting Malmö for the first time? These local tips can help you make the most of your stay.

Residents often follow a sauna session at Ribersborgs Kallbadhus with a chilly swim.

### Getting around the city  
Many of Malmö’s main sights can be reached on foot. Because the city is flat and has many dedicated cycling routes, it is also especially easy to explore by bicycle. Bike hire costs about 120 kronor. Another option is to use the city’s environmentally friendly buses, which run throughout Malmö. Maps are available from the tourist office at Central Station. If you decide to take a taxi, agree on the fare with the driver before the journey begins.

### A chilly tradition  
For over 100 years, Malmö locals have gone to Ribersborgs Kallbadhus to enjoy the sauna and then cool off in the Baltic Sea. The bathing facility stays open throughout the year. To experience it the way many residents do, visit in winter and take an icy dip. Travelers who prefer something milder may enjoy going in summer, when the baths are also open for sunbathing.

### Green living  
Malmö’s reinvention after its industrial era has helped it become known for environmentally conscious design. One example is Bo01, a waterfront housing and redevelopment project centered on sustainable living. To see more examples of modern green planning, explore the Western Harbor and Augustenborg areas. For deeper insight, you can contact the local Environmental Department, which sometimes provides free guided tours of Malmö’s eco-friendly districts.

### Exploring the Sound  
Malmö is only 35 minutes by train from Copenhagen, Denmark’s capital. Thousands of people travel daily between the two cities across the Oresund Bridge. For most of the day, trains depart Malmö every 20 minutes, though departures become less frequent after midnight.

Together, Malmö and Copenhagen form part of the Oresund region, a cross-border Scandinavian area that includes southern Sweden and eastern Denmark. A convenient way to travel around it is with an “Around the Sound” ticket. This pass covers the trains needed to move through the region, including the journey over the Oresund Bridge. You may stop as often as you like, provided you continue traveling in one direction. The tickets are valid for two days and also include discounts at major regional attractions. Prices vary according to distance, beginning at 199 kronor.

### Eating crayfish  
Crayfish are a Swedish favorite, and as summer ends, outdoor crayfish celebrations take place across the country. In Malmö, one of the world’s largest crayfish parties is held in Stortorget, the city’s central square. This large annual event marks the start of the popular Malmö Festival.

In Sweden, crayfish are typically boiled in salty water flavored with dill. To eat them like the locals, have them cold with toast and beer. For an even more traditional experience, pair the meal with akvavit, a Scandinavian spirit similar to vodka.

Malmö is one of the easiest Scandinavian cities for a first-time visitor to settle into. Compact, relaxed, and environmentally minded, it rewards slow exploration as much as efficient planning. Whether you are arriving for a weekend break, using the city as a base for visiting Copenhagen, or beginning a wider journey around southern Sweden, Malmö offers a practical mix of good public transport, walkable neighborhoods, cycling culture, local traditions, and quick regional train links.

A good way to begin is on foot. Malmö’s central areas are not large, and many of the city’s most interesting sights are within comfortable walking distance of one another. Start around Malmö Central Station, then wander toward Stortorget and Lilla Torg, two historic squares that introduce you to the city’s old center. Lilla Torg is especially popular for cafés, restaurants, and outdoor seating in warmer months. From there, you can continue through the shopping streets, pass older brick buildings and modern Scandinavian design stores, and make your way toward Malmöhus Castle and the surrounding parks.

Walking also helps you understand Malmö’s character. The city is not defined by one postcard view but by a mix of old and new: medieval streets, industrial waterfronts, green public spaces, immigrant-owned food shops, contemporary architecture, and seaside promenades. The Western Harbour, or Västra Hamnen, is a particularly good example. Once an industrial area, it has been transformed into one of the city’s most sustainable neighborhoods, known for energy-efficient buildings, waterside paths, swimming spots, and views across the Öresund toward Denmark. The Turning Torso, Malmö’s twisting landmark tower, rises above the area and is visible from many parts of the city.

Cycling is another excellent way to get around. Malmö is one of Sweden’s most bike-friendly cities, with flat terrain, extensive cycle lanes, and a local culture that treats cycling as normal everyday transport rather than a sport. Visitors can rent bikes from shops or use local bike-share options when available. Cycling is especially useful if you want to move between the old center, the beach at Ribersborg, Möllevången, Västra Hamnen, and the parks without relying on buses or taxis. Just remember to follow local cycling rules, use lights after dark, and keep to designated lanes where possible.

For longer distances or bad weather, Malmö’s buses are reliable and easy to use. The city’s public transport is run as part of the Skånetrafiken network, which also covers regional trains throughout Skåne. Tickets are usually bought through the Skånetrafiken app or at machines and service points, rather than from the driver. Buses connect the central station with residential neighborhoods, shopping areas, beaches, and cultural venues. For a first visit, it is worth downloading the transport app in advance so you can check routes, departure times, and ticket options.

Taxis are available but are generally more expensive than public transport. They can be useful late at night, when carrying luggage, or if you are traveling to a specific address that is not convenient by bus. As in much of Sweden, it is best to use established taxi companies or app-based services and to check the fare information before starting your journey. For most daytime sightseeing, however, walking, cycling, and buses are usually simpler and more economical.

One of Malmö’s most distinctive local pleasures is its bathing culture. The city’s seaside location makes swimming and sauna visits part of everyday life for many residents. Ribersborgs Kallbadhus, often called “Kallis,” is a classic open-air bathhouse on the water, with saunas, sea bathing, and a strong local atmosphere. It is especially memorable in winter, when brave bathers alternate between hot sauna rooms and cold dips in the Öresund. Even if you are not sure about cold bathing, visiting a bathhouse is a good way to experience a very Swedish tradition. In summer, Ribersborg beach is also a popular place for sunbathing, swimming, picnics, and evening walks.

Malmö is also known for its green spaces and environmentally conscious planning. Kungsparken and Slottsparken, near Malmöhus Castle, are ideal for a gentle stroll, a picnic, or a break between museum visits. Pildammsparken, a little farther south, is one of the city’s largest parks and is popular with joggers, families, and anyone looking for open space. In Västra Hamnen, the eco-friendly urban design shows another side of Malmö’s green identity, with waterfront paths, innovative housing, and public spaces designed around sustainability.

To understand the city beyond its polished center, spend time in Möllevången, often simply called “Möllan.” This diverse and lively neighborhood is known for its market square, international grocery stores, casual restaurants, bars, and street life. It is one of the best areas in Malmö for affordable food and a more local, multicultural atmosphere. Here you can find falafel, Middle Eastern bakeries, Asian restaurants, Swedish cafés, and independent shops within a few blocks. Malmö’s food scene reflects the city’s diversity, and Möllan is one of the best places to experience it.

Malmö’s location is one of its greatest advantages. The city is connected to Copenhagen by the Öresund Bridge, and trains run frequently between Malmö Central Station and Copenhagen Central Station, with stops at Copenhagen Airport along the way. The journey to the airport is short and straightforward, which makes Malmö a convenient base even for travelers flying in or out of Denmark. Copenhagen can be visited as an easy day trip, while Malmö offers a quieter and often more affordable place to stay.

Regional trains also make it simple to explore Skåne, Sweden’s southernmost region. From Malmö, you can travel to Lund, a charming university city with a famous cathedral and historic streets, in around 10 to 15 minutes by train. Ystad, known for its half-timbered houses and coastal atmosphere, is also within reach. Other destinations, including Helsingborg, Landskrona, and smaller coastal towns, can be visited without renting a car. This makes Malmö a practical hub for travelers who want to experience more of southern Sweden while keeping their plans flexible.

First-time visitors should also be aware of a few local habits. Sweden is largely cashless, so bring a payment card that works internationally. English is widely spoken, especially in shops, restaurants, hotels, and transport settings, so communication is rarely difficult. Tipping is appreciated but not expected in the same way as in some countries; rounding up or leaving a small amount for good service is enough. The weather can change quickly, especially near the water, so layers and a windproof jacket are useful even in mild seasons.

Malmö is not a city that demands a packed checklist. Its appeal lies in how easy it is to move through daily life like a local: walking along canals, cycling to the beach, taking a sauna by the sea, eating in a neighborhood restaurant, browsing markets, and hopping on a train to another city when the mood strikes. It combines accessibility with cultural variety, modern sustainability with old traditions, and Swedish calm with international energy.

For travelers visiting the Öresund region for the first time, Malmö is both a destination and a gateway. It offers enough museums, parks, food, architecture, and waterfront life to fill several days, while its transport links make Copenhagen and the rest of Skåne feel close at hand. Easy to navigate, open in spirit, and deeply connected to its surroundings, Malmö is an ideal base for discovering the best of southern Sweden and its cross-border relationship with Denmark.

# Malmö, Sweden: A First-Timer’s Guide to the Green, Global City by the Bridge

Compact, creative and quietly cool, Malmö is Sweden’s southern gateway — a seaside city where medieval squares meet modern eco-districts, falafel is practically a civic institution, and Copenhagen is close enough for an afternoon coffee run.

For first-time visitors, Malmö offers an easy introduction to Scandinavian life without the crowds or prices of Stockholm. It’s walkable, bike-friendly, diverse and relaxed — a place where you can swim in the sea before breakfast, browse design shops by lunch, and cross an international border by train before dinner.

Here’s how to make the most of it.

---

## Getting Around: Trains, Bikes and the Art of Not Rushing

Malmö is one of Sweden’s easiest cities to navigate. The center is compact, public transport is efficient, and cycling is often the fastest way to get around.

### Arriving in Malmö

Most international visitors arrive through **Copenhagen Airport**, which is actually more convenient for Malmö than many Swedish airports. From the airport, the train to **Malmö Central Station** takes about **20–25 minutes**, crossing the dramatic **Øresund Bridge** between Denmark and Sweden.

You can also arrive by train from **Stockholm**, **Gothenburg**, **Lund** or other Swedish cities.

### Public transportation

Malmö’s buses and regional trains are run through **Skånetrafiken**, the public transport authority for Skåne, Sweden’s southernmost region.

**Insider tip:** Download the **Skånetrafiken app** before you arrive. It’s the easiest way to buy tickets for buses, trains, airport connections and trips to nearby towns. You can use it for travel within Malmö and across the region.

If you’re going to Copenhagen, check ticket rules carefully — cross-border travel has its own fare zones, and you may need ID when crossing between Denmark and Sweden.

### Cycling like a local

Malmö is extremely bike-friendly, with wide lanes and flat terrain. Many hotels rent bikes, and there are bike-share options in the city.

Great cycling routes include:

- **Malmöhus Castle to Ribersborg Beach**
- **Västra Hamnen waterfront loop**
- **Pildammsparken and Slottsparken**
- The path toward **Limhamn** for sea views

**Local etiquette:** Stay in the bike lane, signal with your hand when turning, and don’t stop suddenly in the middle of the path. Malmö cyclists are calmer than Copenhagen’s, but they still expect you to know what you’re doing.

---

## Where to Stay: From Historic Center to Waterfront Cool

### Gamla Staden: Best for first-timers

Malmö’s Old Town is the easiest base for a first visit. You’ll be near **Malmö Central Station**, **Lilla Torg**, **Stortorget**, restaurants, shops and museums.

It’s ideal if you want to walk everywhere and take day trips by train.

### Västra Hamnen: Best for design, sea air and sustainability

Once an industrial harbor, **Västra Hamnen** is now Malmö’s showcase eco-district. It’s home to the twisting **Turning Torso**, waterfront promenades, swimming platforms and energy-efficient architecture.

Stay here if you want modern hotels, sea views and a quieter atmosphere.

### Möllevången: Best for food and nightlife

Known locally as **Möllan**, this multicultural neighborhood is Malmö at its most energetic. Expect produce markets, bars, Middle Eastern bakeries, Asian restaurants, record shops and late-night falafel.

It’s lively, diverse and less polished than the Old Town — in the best way.

---

## What to See: Malmö’s Essential Stops

### Lilla Torg

Malmö’s postcard-perfect little square is lined with half-timbered buildings, outdoor restaurants and bars. It’s touristy, yes, but still atmospheric — especially in the evening.

### Stortorget

The city’s grand main square, home to historic buildings and a statue of King Karl X Gustav. It’s a good orientation point and often hosts events.

### Malmöhus Castle

One of Scandinavia’s oldest surviving Renaissance castles, **Malmöhus** now houses museums covering art, history and natural science. It’s a strong rainy-day option and pairs well with a walk through nearby parks.

### Kungsparken and Slottsparken

These neighboring parks are perfect for a slow stroll, picnic or coffee break. Locals use them year-round, from summer lounging to crisp winter walks.

### Ribersborg Beach

Known as **“Ribban,”** this long sandy beach is where Malmö comes to swim, sunbathe, jog and barbecue. On clear days, you can see the Øresund Bridge stretching toward Denmark.

Don’t miss **Ribersborgs Kallbadhus**, the historic open-air bathhouse at the end of a pier. It offers saunas and cold plunges in the sea — a very Swedish ritual.

**Insider tip:** Swimwear rules vary depending on sauna sections and times, and nudity is common in traditional Swedish bathhouses. Check the rules before entering, and don’t be surprised by the relaxed attitude.

### Västra Hamnen and Turning Torso

The **Turning Torso**, designed by Santiago Calatrava, is Malmö’s modern icon. You can’t generally tour the inside, but the surrounding waterfront is worth visiting for architecture, sea views and sunset walks.

---

## Green Malmö: Neighborhoods and Sustainable Living

Malmö has built a reputation as one of Europe’s greener urban destinations. It’s not just about parks — sustainability is woven into housing, transport and food culture.

### Västra Hamnen

This former industrial area became a model for sustainable urban development. Expect renewable energy systems, thoughtful public spaces, bike-first streets and waterfront access.

It’s especially beautiful at sunset, when locals gather on wooden decks with takeout, blankets and drinks.

### Augustenborg

Less visited by tourists, **Augustenborg** is known for its eco-renovation projects, green roofs and stormwater management. It’s an interesting area for travelers curious about urban sustainability beyond the postcard sights.

### Sege Park

An emerging green neighborhood with a focus on sustainability, community spaces and reuse. It’s still developing, but it reflects Malmö’s ongoing push toward climate-conscious urban life.

### Parks to explore

- **Pildammsparken**: Malmö’s grand park, ideal for jogging and picnics  
- **Folkets Park**: A lively “people’s park” with cafés, events and family activities  
- **Slottsparken**: Central, scenic and easy to combine with Malmöhus Castle  
- **Kungsparken**: Romantic, leafy and perfect for a slow walk  

---

## Food: Falafel, Fika and Seasonal Swedish Traditions

Malmö’s food scene reflects both southern Swedish traditions and the city’s global population. You’ll find New Nordic dining, immigrant-run bakeries, natural wine bars, street food and some of Sweden’s best falafel.

### The Malmö must-eat: falafel

Malmö is famous in Sweden for falafel, thanks to its large Middle Eastern community and affordable street-food culture. You’ll find falafel shops all over town, especially around **Möllevången**.

Order it in a wrap with pickled vegetables, tahini, chili sauce and fresh herbs.

**Insider tip:** Ask locals where they go — everyone has a favorite, and opinions can be passionate.

### Fika: coffee and something sweet

The Swedish coffee break is not optional — it’s a way of life. Order coffee with a cinnamon bun, cardamom bun or pastry and linger without guilt.

Good areas for fika include:

- **Gamla Väster**
- **Davidshall**
- **Möllevången**
- **Västra Hamnen**

### Seasonal food traditions

Swedish cuisine is deeply tied to the calendar, and Malmö follows the rhythm with southern charm.

#### Spring: waffles and asparagus

Around **March 25**, Swedes celebrate **Våffeldagen** — Waffle Day — with waffles, whipped cream and jam. Spring also brings tender asparagus and early greens from Skåne’s fertile farmland.

#### Late spring and early summer: new potatoes and strawberries

By June, look for **färskpotatis** — Swedish new potatoes — often served with dill, butter and herring. Local strawberries arrive around the same time and are a centerpiece of summer celebrations.

#### Midsummer: herring, potatoes and snaps

**Midsummer**, usually celebrated in late June, is one of Sweden’s biggest holidays. Expect pickled herring, new potatoes, sour cream, chives, strawberries and schnapps songs.

If you’re visiting then, many shops and restaurants may close or reduce hours as locals head to countryside gatherings.

#### August: crayfish parties

In late summer, Swedes celebrate **kräftskiva**, or crayfish parties. The traditional setup includes crayfish, paper hats, lanterns, snaps and singing. Some restaurants offer crayfish menus, though the most authentic versions happen in homes and gardens.

#### Autumn: mushrooms, apples and goose

Skåne is known for apples, and autumn brings apple cakes, ciders and harvest menus. Around **Mårten Gås** in November, southern Sweden traditionally serves roast goose with rich accompaniments — a tradition especially associated with Skåne.

#### December: saffron buns and Christmas tables

In December, bakeries fill with **lussekatter**, saffron buns tied to Lucia celebrations on December 13. Restaurants may serve **julbord**, the Swedish Christmas buffet, with herring, salmon, meatballs, ham, cheeses and sweets.

---

## Local Customs: How to Blend In

Swedes are friendly but often reserved. Malmö is more relaxed and multicultural than some other Swedish cities, but a few customs still apply.

### Respect personal space

People generally don’t chat with strangers in queues or on buses. A smile is fine; prolonged small talk may surprise people.

### Queue properly

Sweden is serious about queues. Look for ticket-number systems in bakeries, pharmacies and service counters.

### Take your shoes off indoors

If invited to someone’s home, remove your shoes at the door unless told otherwise.

### Be punctual

If you book a table or meet someone, be on time. “A little late” is still late.

### Tap water is excellent

Ask for tap water confidently. It’s clean, free in many restaurants, and widely preferred.

### English is widely spoken

You can get by easily in English, but a few Swedish words go a long way:

- **Hej** — Hello  
- **Tack** — Thank you  
- **Ursäkta** — Excuse me  
- **Fika** — Coffee break  
- **Lagom** — Not too much, not too little; just right  

---

## Day Trip to Copenhagen: Two Countries, One Easy Train Ride

One of Malmö’s biggest advantages is its proximity to Copenhagen. The train from **Malmö Central** to **Copenhagen Central Station** usually takes about **35–45 minutes**, making Denmark’s capital an easy day trip.

### How to go

Take the Øresundståg train from Malmö Central. Trains are frequent, and you can buy tickets through the Skånetrafiken app or station machines.

**Insider tip:** Bring your passport or national ID. Border checks are not always constant, but they can happen.

### What to do in Copenhagen in one day

For a classic first visit:

- Start at **Nyhavn** for colorful harbor views  
- Walk or bike to **Amalienborg Palace**  
- Visit **Rosenborg Castle** or the **National Museum of Denmark**  
- Eat at a food market such as **Torvehallerne**  
- Explore **Christianshavn** or **Vesterbro**  
- End with a walk through **Tivoli Gardens** if it’s open  

### A more local Copenhagen day

Skip the biggest sights and spend the day around:

- **Nørrebro** for independent shops and food  
- **Vesterbro** for cafés, bars and design  
- **Refshaleøen** for harbor swimming, street food and industrial-cool spaces  

### Currency note

Sweden uses the **Swedish krona**, while Denmark uses the **Danish krone**. Cards are widely accepted in both countries, so you probably won’t need cash.

---

## Other Easy Day Trips from Malmö

### Lund

Just 10–15 minutes by train, **Lund** is one of Sweden’s prettiest university towns. Visit **Lund Cathedral**, wander cobbled streets and enjoy the student-town café culture.

### Ystad

A charming coastal town known for pastel-colored houses, cobbled lanes and as the setting for the “Wallander” detective stories.

### Falsterbo and Skanör

These seaside towns at the southwestern tip of Sweden are known for white sand beaches, colorful beach huts and birdwatching. Best in summer.

### Helsingborg

A coastal city north of Malmö with a waterfront, castle tower and ferry connections to Helsingør in Denmark.

### Ven

A small island in the Øresund, ideal for cycling in summer. Ferries run from Landskrona, reachable by train from Malmö.

---

## When to Visit Malmö

### Spring

Cool, fresh and increasingly bright. Parks come alive, outdoor cafés reopen and the city feels optimistic.

### Summer

The best season for beaches, cycling, outdoor dining and long evenings. Days are long, and locals spend as much time outside as possible.

### Autumn

A cozy time for food, culture and fewer crowds. Expect golden leaves, harvest flavors and crisp walks by the sea.

### Winter

Dark and chilly, but atmospheric. Christmas markets, candles, saunas and cafés make the season feel intimate. Pack warm layers and waterproof shoes.

---

## Practical Tips for First-Time Visitors

- **Best length of stay:** 2–3 days, or longer if using Malmö as a base for Copenhagen and Skåne  
- **Best area to stay:** Gamla Staden for convenience; Västra Hamnen for waterfront calm  
- **Best free activity:** Walk from Malmö Central to Ribersborg Beach via the parks and waterfront  
- **Best local experience:** Sauna and cold plunge at Ribersborgs Kallbadhus  
- **Best food neighborhood:** Möllevången  
- **Best sunset spot:** Västra Hamnen waterfront  
- **Best easy day trip:** Lund or Copenhagen  

---

## The Takeaway

Malmö doesn’t shout for attention. It rewards travelers who slow down, rent a bike, try the falafel, wander beyond the main square and sit by the water watching trains glide across the Øresund Bridge.

For first-time visitors, it offers a rare combination: Scandinavian design, global food, green city planning, seaside living and effortless access to another country. It’s Sweden with a southern accent — relaxed, open-minded and just the right size for discovery.

# First trip to Malmo?

Malmo is one of Sweden’s easiest cities to enjoy on a first visit: compact, bike-friendly, relaxed, and full of seaside views, modern architecture, cafés, parks, and quick connections to Copenhagen. Here are practical tips to help you make the most of your trip.

## Start with the city’s easygoing vibe

Malmo is Sweden’s third-largest city, but it feels manageable rather than overwhelming. The center is walkable, many attractions are close together, and the city has a welcoming mix of old squares, canals, beaches, and modern neighborhoods. A good first-day plan is to wander around **Lilla Torg**, **Stortorget**, and the old town area, then continue toward the water for a completely different side of the city.

## Visit Ribersborgs Kallbadhus

One of Malmo’s classic experiences is **Ribersborgs Kallbadhus**, often called “Kallis.” This historic open-air bathhouse sits out on a pier by Ribersborg Beach and is famous for saunas, cold sea dips, and views across the Oresund.

It’s a very Swedish experience: warm up in the sauna, step outside, take a dip in the sea, then repeat. Many areas are traditionally clothing-optional and separated by gender, though arrangements can vary, so check current rules before you go. Even if you’re not used to cold bathing, it’s worth trying—especially followed by coffee, lunch, or a quiet moment looking over the water.

**Tip:** Bring a towel, sandals or flip-flops, and an open mind. In colder months, the contrast between hot sauna and icy water is part of the fun.

## Get around by bike and bus

Malmo is excellent for cycling. The city is flat, bike lanes are common, and distances are short. Renting a bike is one of the best ways to explore neighborhoods, parks, beaches, and the waterfront without rushing.

If you prefer public transport, buses are reliable and useful for reaching areas outside the center. Local transport is run through **Skånetrafiken**, and tickets are usually bought through the app or ticket machines rather than from the driver. The same regional system also connects Malmo with Lund, Copenhagen Airport, and Copenhagen.

**Practical advice:**
- Use a bike for short trips and waterfront exploring.
- Use buses when the weather turns or you’re heading farther out.
- Download the Skånetrafiken app before arrival.
- If cycling, follow local bike signals and stay out of pedestrian-only zones.

## Explore Bo01 and the Western Harbor

For a glimpse of modern Malmo, head to **Bo01** in the **Western Harbor**. This waterfront district was developed with sustainability and contemporary architecture in mind, and it’s one of the best places in the city for a scenic walk or bike ride.

You’ll find sleek apartment buildings, canals, swimming spots, boardwalks, and open views of the water. The area is also home to the **Turning Torso**, Malmo’s twisting landmark skyscraper. Even if you don’t go inside, it’s worth seeing from the outside as part of a waterfront stroll.

In summer, the Western Harbor is especially lively, with people sunbathing, swimming, picnicking, and watching the sunset. It’s also a good area to bring takeaway food and enjoy a simple meal by the sea.

## See the Oresund Bridge

The **Oresund Bridge** is one of the region’s most impressive sights, linking Sweden and Denmark across the Oresund Strait. You can see it from several points along Malmo’s coast, especially around Ribersborg Beach and the Western Harbor on clear days.

If you have time, consider taking the train across the bridge to Copenhagen. The journey is quick and easy, making Malmo a great base for visiting both Sweden and Denmark in one trip. Just remember that you’re crossing an international border, so carry valid ID or a passport.

**Tip:** For photos, try the waterfront near Ribersborg or viewpoints around the Western Harbor, especially around sunset.

## Try seasonal food traditions, including crayfish parties

If you’re visiting in late summer, you may hear about Swedish **crayfish parties**, or *kräftskivor*. These festive gatherings usually happen in August and early autumn, when people eat crayfish, wear paper hats, sing drinking songs, and enjoy a cheerful, slightly silly atmosphere.

As a visitor, you might find crayfish-themed menus in restaurants, supermarket crayfish kits, or local events. If you’re invited to a private crayfish party, say yes—it’s a memorable cultural experience. Expect cold crayfish, bread, cheese, snaps, beer, and plenty of singing.

**Tip:** Crayfish can be messy to eat, so don’t wear your most delicate outfit.

## Enjoy parks, cafés, and local neighborhoods

Malmo is also a city for slow travel. Spend time in **Kungsparken** and **Slottsparken**, two lovely green areas near Malmo Castle. Visit **Malmöhus Castle** if you’re interested in history, museums, or traveling with children. For cafés, small shops, and a local feel, explore areas like **Möllevången**, known for its multicultural food scene and lively market square.

Malmo is a good place to eat casually. You’ll find everything from Swedish classics to falafel, Middle Eastern food, Nordic-style bakeries, and modern restaurants. The city is particularly known for affordable, tasty falafel, so it’s worth grabbing one during your stay.

## When to visit

Summer brings long days, swimming, outdoor dining, and the best chance of warm weather. Late summer is ideal if you’re curious about crayfish parties. Spring and early autumn are also pleasant for biking and sightseeing. Winter is quieter and colder, but saunas, cafés, and museums make it cozy.

Because Malmo is coastal, wind can make temperatures feel cooler than expected. Pack layers, even in summer, and bring a rain jacket if you plan to cycle.

## Simple first-time itinerary

**Day 1:** Explore the old town, Lilla Torg, parks, and Malmo Castle.  
**Day 2:** Bike to Ribersborg Beach, try Ribersborgs Kallbadhus, then continue to Bo01 and the Western Harbor.  
**Day 3:** Take in views of the Oresund Bridge or ride the train to Copenhagen for a day trip.

## Final tips for your first trip

Malmo rewards a relaxed pace. Don’t overplan every hour—rent a bike, follow the waterfront, stop for coffee, and enjoy the mix of Swedish calm, international flavor, and seaside scenery. Between cold bathing at Ribersborgs Kallbadhus, cycling through the Western Harbor, spotting the Oresund Bridge, and maybe joining a crayfish party, your first trip to Malmo can feel both easy and distinctly local.

# Malmö Travel Guide: Sea Baths, Green Living and Festival Food in Sweden’s Southern Gateway

Malmö, Sweden’s third-largest city, has become one of Scandinavia’s easiest urban escapes: compact, bike-friendly, multicultural and linked directly to Copenhagen by the Øresund Bridge. For visitors, it offers a mix of seaside bathing culture, forward-looking eco districts, strong food markets and summer festivals — all within a city that is simple to navigate without a car.

## Start with Malmö’s bathing culture

Malmö’s relationship with the sea is central to local life, especially in warmer months when residents head to the waterfront before work, after work and late into the long Nordic evenings.

The classic stop is **Ribersborgs Kallbadhus**, often called “Kallis,” a traditional open-air bathhouse dating back to the late 19th century. Set on a pier off Ribersborg Beach, it offers saunas, cold plunges into the Øresund and separate bathing areas, with a relaxed café and sea views. Cold bathing is popular year-round, and winter visitors will see that the local commitment to a dip does not disappear when temperatures fall.

Nearby **Ribersborg Beach**, sometimes nicknamed “Ribban,” is Malmö’s urban seaside playground: a long sandy stretch with grassy areas, walking paths and views across the water toward the Øresund Bridge. In summer, it is one of the best places to understand the city’s easygoing outdoor culture.

For a more contemporary swim, head to **Scaniabadet** in the Western Harbour, where wooden decks and ladders lead straight into the sea. It is especially popular with younger locals and offers striking views of the waterfront and the Turning Torso tower.

## Eco-friendly Malmö: where sustainability is part of the itinerary

Malmö has spent years building a reputation as one of Europe’s greener city-break destinations. Its best-known example is **Västra Hamnen**, or the Western Harbour, a former industrial docklands area transformed into a sustainable residential and leisure district.

Visitors can walk or cycle through the area to see energy-efficient housing, waterfront promenades and green public spaces. The district’s landmark is **Turning Torso**, the twisting residential tower designed by Santiago Calatrava and one of Malmö’s most recognizable silhouettes.

Another eco-focused stop is **Augustenborg**, a residential district known for green roofs, open stormwater channels and climate-adaptation planning. It is less touristy than the waterfront, but useful for visitors interested in urban sustainability and how cities are preparing for heavier rainfall and climate change.

For green downtime, visit **Kungsparken** and **Slottsparken**, central parks that form a leafy corridor around Malmö Castle. They are ideal for walking, picnicking or taking a break between museum visits. The nearby **Malmöhus Castle** complex includes museums and exhibitions, making it an easy half-day stop.

## Getting around: bikes, buses and trains

Malmö is one of the easiest Swedish cities to explore without a car. The city is flat, distances are short and cycling infrastructure is extensive. Renting a bike is often the best way to move between the central station, the old town, the parks, Ribersborg Beach and the Western Harbour.

Public transport is also straightforward. Local buses and regional trains are operated within the Skåne transport network, and tickets can generally be bought through the **Skånetrafiken** app. Malmö Central Station is the main rail hub, with trains running to nearby towns such as Lund, Helsingborg and Ystad.

For visitors staying centrally, many highlights are walkable: **Lilla Torg**, **Stortorget**, Malmöhus Castle, the parks and shopping streets are all close together. To reach the beach or Västra Hamnen, cycling or a short bus ride is usually fastest.

## Copenhagen access: across the Øresund Bridge

One of Malmö’s biggest advantages is its direct link to Denmark. The **Øresund Bridge** connects Malmö with Copenhagen, making it possible to visit two countries in one trip.

Trains run frequently between **Malmö Central Station** and **Copenhagen Central Station**, with journey times typically around 35–45 minutes depending on the service. Copenhagen Airport is even closer, often around 20–25 minutes by train from Malmö. This makes Malmö a practical base for travelers flying into Denmark but looking for a calmer, often more affordable place to stay.

Border checks can occasionally affect travel times, so visitors should carry valid identification and allow extra time when heading to the airport or onward connections.

## What to eat at the Malmö Festival

The **Malmö Festival**, usually held in August, is one of the city’s biggest annual events, filling the center with concerts, cultural events and food stalls. It is also one of the best times to sample Malmö’s diverse food scene in one place.

Expect a mix of Swedish classics, street food and international flavors reflecting the city’s multicultural population. Look for:

- **Herring and new potatoes** — a traditional Swedish summer combination, often served simply with dill and sour cream.  
- **Smoked fish** — common in southern Sweden and a good festival option if available from local vendors.  
- **Falafel** — Malmö is famous in Sweden for its falafel, thanks to its strong Middle Eastern food culture. A fresh falafel wrap is practically a local fast-food essential.  
- **Langos** — a festival favorite in Sweden, this fried flatbread is usually topped with sour cream, cheese, onion and sometimes roe.  
- **Skåne-style dishes** — regional flavors may include hearty breads, local cheeses, sausages and seasonal produce.  
- **Cinnamon buns and cardamom buns** — ideal with coffee during a fika break.  
- **Vegetarian and vegan street food** — Malmö has a strong plant-based dining scene, and festival stalls often reflect that.

The festival is busy in the evenings, particularly around major performances. For shorter queues, go earlier in the day, then return after dinner for music and atmosphere.

## Best areas to explore

**Gamla Staden**, the old town, is the natural starting point. Around **Lilla Torg**, cobbled streets, restaurants and terraces create one of Malmö’s liveliest central scenes. **Stortorget**, the larger historic square, gives a more formal view of the city’s past.

**Möllevången**, often called “Möllan,” is the city’s multicultural food district, known for markets, casual restaurants and nightlife. It is one of the best areas for affordable eats, especially falafel, noodles, mezze and late-night snacks.

**Västra Hamnen** is the place for modern Malmö: sea views, contemporary architecture, bathing decks and sunset walks.

## Practical tips for visitors

- **Currency:** Sweden uses the Swedish krona, not the euro. Card payments are widely accepted, and many places are cashless.  
- **Language:** Swedish is the official language, but English is widely spoken.  
- **Best time to visit:** May to September for outdoor dining, cycling and bathing; August for the Malmö Festival.  
- **Pack for weather:** Even in summer, bring layers. Coastal winds can make evenings cool.  
- **Sustainable travel:** Arrive by train if possible, use bikes and public transport, and choose local food markets and eco-conscious hotels.

## The bottom line

Malmö works well as both a standalone city break and a cross-border add-on to Copenhagen. Its appeal lies in the combination of sea baths, cycling culture, sustainable urban design and a food scene shaped by both Swedish tradition and global migration. Come in summer for the full outdoor experience — and if your visit lines up with the Malmö Festival, arrive hungry.

# Malmö Local Insider Advice Guide

Malmö is compact, bike-friendly, seaside, multicultural, and easy to combine with Copenhagen or the rest of Skåne. The best way to enjoy it is to move slowly: cycle between neighborhoods, swim or sauna by the sea, eat casually, and leave time for parks, waterfronts, and spontaneous detours.

---

## 1. Cycling Around the City

Malmö is one of Sweden’s best cities for cycling. It is flat, relatively small, and has a strong network of bike lanes, so you can comfortably use a bike as your main transport.

### Local tips

- **Rent a bike if you’re staying more than a day.** Many hotels offer rentals, and there are local rental shops around the central areas.
- **Use bike lanes confidently.** Malmö cyclists move at a steady pace, so avoid stopping suddenly in bike lanes.
- **Ring your bell before passing pedestrians** on shared paths, especially in parks and along the waterfront.
- **Watch for cobblestones and tram/bus lanes** in older central streets.
- **Lock your bike properly.** Bike theft exists, so use a solid lock and attach the bike to something fixed.

### Good cycling routes

**Central Station → Västra Hamnen → Ribersborg**  
A classic Malmö ride. Start at Malmö C, head toward the waterfront and Västra Hamnen, pass modern architecture and sea views, then continue toward Ribersborg beach.

**Pildammsparken loop**  
A relaxing ride through one of Malmö’s most loved parks. Good for a quieter break from the city center.

**Möllevången → Folkets Park → S:t Knuts torg**  
Great if you want cafés, casual restaurants, independent shops, and a more local neighborhood feel.

**Ribersborg → Limhamn**  
Follow the coast southwest for sea air, views toward the Öresund Bridge, and a calmer residential side of Malmö.

### Insider advice

If the wind is strong, plan your route so the return trip is with the wind behind you. Malmö is flat, but coastal wind can make cycling feel much harder than expected.

---

## 2. Ribersborgs Kallbadhus

Ribersborgs Kallbadhus, often called **“Kallis”**, is one of Malmö’s most iconic local experiences. It is a traditional open-air cold bathhouse on a pier at Ribersborg beach, with saunas, sea bathing, and views across the Öresund.

### What to expect

- You alternate between **hot sauna and cold sea dips**.
- There are usually **separate nude bathing/sauna sections** for men and women, plus sometimes mixed options depending on the setup and schedule.
- It is very normal in Sweden to sauna nude in traditional bathhouses, but check the rules on arrival if you are unsure.
- There is also a café/restaurant, making it a good place to linger.

### When to go

- **Winter:** The most memorable time. Cold air, hot sauna, icy sea, and a very Nordic feeling.
- **Summer:** Still lovely, especially combined with a beach day at Ribersborg.
- **Sunset:** Excellent if you want the best atmosphere and views.

### Local tips

- Bring **two towels** if you can: one to sit on in the sauna and one to dry yourself.
- Bring sandals or flip-flops, especially in colder months.
- Don’t overthink the cold dip. Go in, breathe calmly, and get out when you need to.
- Check opening times and any booking requirements before going, especially around holidays and weekends.

---

## 3. Green Development Areas and Sustainable Malmö

Malmö is known for urban transformation, especially from industrial waterfront to sustainable city districts. If you are interested in architecture, city planning, climate adaptation, or green living, it is worth exploring beyond the old town.

### Västra Hamnen

This former industrial harbor area is Malmö’s flagship sustainable district.

Highlights:

- **Turning Torso**, Malmö’s famous twisting skyscraper.
- Waterfront promenades with views of the Öresund Bridge.
- Energy-efficient housing and urban design projects.
- Swimming platforms and popular summer hangout spots.

Local advice:  
Go in the late afternoon, walk or cycle along the water, then continue toward Ribersborg. On a clear day you get beautiful views toward Copenhagen.

### Bo01 area

Part of Västra Hamnen, **Bo01** was created for a major housing exhibition and is often cited as a model for sustainable urban planning.

Look for:

- Small-scale courtyards and varied architecture.
- Canals, pedestrian lanes, and wind-protected public spaces.
- A mix of dense housing and access to the sea.

Local advice:  
Don’t just look at Turning Torso. Wander into the smaller residential lanes of Bo01; that is where the design becomes more interesting.

### Augustenborg / Ekostaden Augustenborg

Augustenborg is known for climate adaptation and green infrastructure.

Highlights:

- Open stormwater channels.
- Green roofs.
- Urban renewal projects focused on sustainability and social development.

Local advice:  
This is less of a postcard destination and more interesting if you like urban planning. Pair it with nearby neighborhoods or go as part of a self-guided sustainability tour.

### Hyllie

Hyllie is a newer development area near Malmö Arena and Emporia shopping center, close to the train line to Copenhagen.

Highlights:

- Modern high-density development.
- Climate-smart planning ambitions.
- Quick train access to both central Malmö and Copenhagen Airport.

Local advice:  
Hyllie is practical rather than charming, but it shows Malmö’s future-facing growth. It is also useful if you are traveling onward by train.

---

## 4. Around the Sound Tickets

The **Around the Sound** concept refers to traveling in a loop around the Öresund region, usually combining southern Sweden, Denmark, trains, and the Helsingør–Helsingborg ferry. It is a great day trip if you want to see both sides of the Sound without renting a car.

The classic loop is something like:

**Malmö → Copenhagen → Helsingør → ferry to Helsingborg → train back to Malmö**

or the reverse.

### Why do it?

- You see Malmö, Copenhagen, coastal Zealand, Helsingør, Helsingborg, and the Öresund region in one trip.
- The short ferry ride between Helsingør and Helsingborg is scenic and fun.
- It gives you a feel for how connected southern Sweden and eastern Denmark are.

### Suggested route from Malmö

1. Take the train from **Malmö C to Copenhagen**.
2. Spend a few hours in Copenhagen if you want.
3. Continue by train to **Helsingør**.
4. Visit **Kronborg Castle**, famous as Hamlet’s castle.
5. Take the ferry from **Helsingør to Helsingborg**.
6. Walk around Helsingborg or have dinner.
7. Take the train back to **Malmö**.

### Local advice

- Start early if you want to enjoy stops along the way.
- Check current ticket conditions with **Skånetrafiken** and Danish transport providers before you go, because ticket names, validity, and availability can change.
- Bring your passport or national ID. Border checks are not always present, but you are crossing between Sweden and Denmark.
- If you are short on time, prioritize Helsingør and the ferry crossing over trying to “do” Copenhagen properly in the same day.

---

## 5. Traditional Crayfish Celebrations

Swedish crayfish parties, or **kräftskivor**, are a late-summer tradition, usually held in **August and early September**. They are festive, informal, and a little silly in the best way.

### What happens at a kräftskiva?

People gather to eat crayfish, drink, sing drinking songs, wear paper hats, and enjoy the last warm evenings of summer.

Typical elements include:

- **Crayfish**, usually served cold with dill.
- **Västerbotten cheese pie**, a classic side dish.
- Bread, butter, cheese, salads, and sometimes prawns or other seafood.
- **Snaps**, often accompanied by short traditional songs.
- Paper lanterns, bibs, and colorful party hats.

### Local tips for tourists

- If you are invited to a private kräftskiva, say yes. It is one of the most fun Swedish social traditions.
- Be ready to sing. You do not need to know the words perfectly; enthusiasm matters more.
- Crayfish are eaten with your hands, so it is messy by design.
- Drink slowly if snaps are involved. The songs can make the pace deceptive.
- If you want to recreate the experience, supermarkets often sell crayfish party supplies in August.

### Where to experience it

Crayfish parties are usually private, but some restaurants, hotels, or event venues may offer seasonal crayfish menus or themed evenings. Check local listings in Malmö in late summer.

### Insider advice

A proper kräftskiva is not just about the crayfish. It is about the atmosphere: late summer darkness, lanterns, laughter, songs, and a sense that everyone is squeezing the last drops out of the season.

---

## Extra Malmö Tips

- **Neighborhoods to explore:** Möllevången, S:t Knut, Västra Hamnen, Gamla Väster, Davidshall, and Limhamn.
- **Good local food areas:** Möllevångstorget for multicultural casual food, Saluhallen for an easy indoor food hall, and S:t Knut for cafés.
- **Best seaside walk:** Västra Hamnen to Ribersborg.
- **Best relaxed park:** Pildammsparken.
- **Best day trip:** Lund, Copenhagen, or the Around the Sound loop.
- **Best Malmö mindset:** Do less, linger more, and travel by bike.
